spec.full_target: Let n,m be positive integers; u:R^n×(0,∞)→R^m jointly smooth and q∈R^m have Euclidean norm one. Assume |u(x,r)|=1; for each (x,r) there is a∈R with u_tt−Δ_xu=a u; and on each compact interval J⊂(0,∞), u=q outside a compact C_J uniformly for r∈J. Define e(x,r)=|u_t|²+Σ_{j=1}^n|∂_{x_j}u|² and E(r)=∫_{R^n}e(x,r)dx, Lebesgue measure, Euclidean norms. Prove e(·,r) is Lebesgue integrable for each r>0, E is differentiable for each r>0, and E'(r)=0.
spec.conclusion: For every r>0, e(·,r) is Lebesgue integrable, E is differentiable at r, and E'(r)=0.

hypotheses.statement: For all x∈R^n,r>0 there exists a∈R such that u_tt(x,r)-Δ_xu(x,r)=a u(x,r), with componentwise Δ_x.
For each compact interval J⊂(0,∞), there is compact C_J⊂R^n such that u(x,r)=q for x∉C_J and r∈J.

definitions.definition: E(r)=Lebesgue integral over R^n of e(x,r)

calculations: Finite Euclidean inner-product and sum calculations; one-variable fundamental theorem of calculus; compact-box uniform continuity; Fubini for continuous compactly supported functions.

locals.type: compact interval in (0,∞) with r0 in its interior
locals.declaration: Choose a compact interval about r0.
Choose the compact support set supplied by H003 for J.

locals.type: closed box in R^n containing C_J

Write u_t for the time derivative of u.
Write u_{tt} for the second time derivative of u.

argument.text: Fix arbitrary r0>0 and choose a compact interval J about it. By H003 choose compact C_J. The map equals the constant q on the open complement of C_J, so all first derivatives vanish there; continuity implies they vanish on the boundary as well. Thus e(·,r) is continuous, bounded on C_J and zero off C_J, proving its Lebesgue integrability. Choose a closed box B containing C_J. On B, e and its time derivative are continuous; the time derivative is uniformly continuous on B×J. For h→0 the one-variable fundamental theorem of calculus writes the difference quotient of e as the average of its time derivative between r0 and r0+h. Uniform continuity gives uniform convergence on B, so finite measure of B allows integration of the limit. Hence E'(r0)=∫_B e_t(x,r0)dx. Differentiating the finite sum defining e gives e_t=2u_t·u_tt+2Σ_j u_j·∂_j u_t. For each j, the smooth compactly supported scalar product u_t·u_j has spatial derivative whose integral is zero: integrate first in x_j by the one-dimensional fundamental theorem of calculus, then in the other variables by Fubini, applicable since the derivative is continuous and compactly supported. Thus ∫u_j·∂_j u_t=−∫u_t·∂_j u_j. Summing yields E'(r0)=2∫u_t·(u_tt−Δ_xu). Differentiating |u|²=1 once in time gives u·u_t=0. By H002, pointwise u_tt−Δ_xu=a u for some scalar a; hence u_t·(u_tt−Δ_xu)=0. The integral is zero. Since r0 was arbitrary the conclusion holds for every positive time.
